passage:
"Baba, why do birds fly in a V?" said Payal, standing beside the desk.
"Hmm?" said Amandeep, eyes on the laptop. "Something about air. I'll tell you later."
"And why does the moon follow the car?"
"It doesn't, really."
"But why does it seem to?"
"Payal, I'm working."
"Baba, why is your screen bright?"
Amandeep stopped typing and looked at Payal. "You're asking a lot of questions. Are they about the birds, or about me?"
Payal shrugged, and said softly, "I don't want you to look at the laptop."
"Okay. Give me ten minutes, then I'm all yours."

qa.q: What did Payal ask about birds?
qa.a: Why birds fly in a V.

qa.q: What was Payal really wanting when asking about the bright screen?
qa.a: Payal felt ignored and wanted Baba's attention, softly saying, 'I don't want you to look at the laptop.'

qa.q: What small step helped Payal and Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep noticed the need for connection and promised a set time to give full attention after finishing the work.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt when Payal said "I don't want you to look at the laptop"?
qa.a: Touched and a bit guilty, realising the questions were about connection, so Amandeep stopped typing and promised ten minutes.

grounding: A child asks many questions to keep an adult engaged rather than because of the topic, and noticing the need for connection reduces the pressure.

passage: My name is Nirmala. When I was nine, I used to follow Nani Sudha around the kitchen asking things. "Why does rice swell? Where does steam go? Why is the pot black?" I didn't really care about the answers. Nani would answer patiently and keep chopping. One day she put down the knife, wiped her hands and looked at me. "Nirmala, I think you want me to stay with you. Is that right?" My face went hot, but I nodded. She smiled, pulled up a stool and said, "Come, tell me about your day, and I'll chop and listen." That afternoon I stopped asking about steam and talked about my friend's lost pencil box.

qa.q: Whose kitchen did Nirmala follow Nani Sudha around?
What was Nirmala really feeling when asking about rice and steam?
qa.a: Mostly a wish for Nani's company rather than the answers; when Nani named it, Nirmala's face went hot with embarrassment.

qa.q: What did Nani Sudha do that changed the pattern?
qa.a: Nani put down the knife, named that Nirmala might want company, and invited Nirmala to talk about the day while chopping.

qa.q: How might Nani Sudha have seen the questions before noticing?
qa.a: As ordinary curiosity, answered patiently, until Nani realised they were a way to stay close.

grounding: A child asks many questions to keep an adult engaged, not because of the topic, and the adult responds to the need for connection.
